gloss: be light, slight, swift; make light of; curse
summary: The root is lightness, the opposite of כָּבֵד “heavy, honoured”. A light thing is easy, of little weight or account, and quick: the waters were “lightened” from the earth, a man is “light of foot” like a gazelle, Hagar's mistress became “light in her eyes”, and Rehoboam's people asked him to “make light” their heavy yoke. To make a man light by word is to treat him with contempt, and so the piel קִלֵּל is to curse: to revile parents, rulers or God, or to call down evil on someone, the opposite of בֵּרַךְ “bless” (Gen 12:3; Psa 109:28). The noun קְלָלָה is a curse, above all the curse set before Israel beside the blessing (Deu 30:19), and the hanged man is “קִלְלַת אֱלֹהִים” (Deu 21:23), which Paul applies to Christ (Gal 3:13). Akkadian qalālu “be light, belittle, despise”, Arabic qalla “be few, little”, the Aramaic of the Targums and the Peshitta, and Ge'ez share the sense of lightness.

words.gloss: be light, slight, swift; make light; curse
words.summary: About eighty times. In the qal and niphal it is to be light: of little weight (waters abating), of little account (despised in the eyes), easy, or quick. The hiphil makes a thing light, a load or a yoke, or makes a man of no account. The piel, the commonest stem, makes light of someone by word: to revile or curse; its pual is to be cursed. The reduplicated pilpel and hithpalpel are to shake, to move to and fro, and to whet or polish. No cognate yet shows the pilpel and hithpalpel senses (shake, move to and fro, whet), so they stand on four verses and their contexts, and their tie to the root is not shown.

stems.gloss: be light; abate; be swift; be slight, despised

senses.definition: Of the flood waters: to grow less, to be lightened from off the earth.

evidence.note: Noah sent the dove “to see הֲקַלּוּ הַמַּיִם”, whether the waters were lightened from the face of the ground.
With the olive leaf, “Noah knew כִּי־קַלּוּ הַמַּיִם מֵעַל הָאָרֶץ”.

senses.definition: To be light in motion, quick: of men, horses and days, nearly always compared with something proverbially fast (eagles, leopards, a runner, a shuttle).

evidence.note: Saul and Jonathan: “מִנְּשָׁרִים קַלּוּ, מֵאֲרָיוֹת גָּבֵרוּ”, swifter than eagles, stronger than lions.
“My days קַלּוּ מִנִּי־רָץ”, swifter than a runner; they flee.
“My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and come to an end without hope.”
“His horses קַלּוּ מִנְּשָׁרִים.”
The Chaldeans' horses “are swifter than leopards”.

senses.gloss: be slight, of little account; be despised (in the eyes of)
senses.definition: To be light in worth or standing: to count for little in another's eyes, or to be of no account. The opposite is to be heavy, honoured (כָּבֵד).

evidence.note: When Hagar saw she had conceived, “וַתֵּקַל גְּבִרְתָּהּ בְּעֵינֶיהָ”, her mistress was light in her eyes.
Sarai: “וָאֵקַל בְּעֵינֶיהָ.”
“מְכַבְּדַי אֲכַבֵּד וּבֹזַי יֵקָלּוּ”: those who honour me I will honour, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed.
Job before God: “הֵן קַלֹּתִי”, behold, I am of small account; what shall I answer you?
To Nineveh's king: “I will make your grave, כִּי קַלּוֹתָ”, for you are worthless.

stems.gloss: be a light thing, easy; lightly; abase oneself; be swift

senses.gloss: be a light thing, easy, a small matter
senses.definition: Of a task or a deed: to be light, easy, a trifle, usually “in the eyes of” someone; in a question, “is it too light a thing?”

evidence.note: “וְנָקַל זֹאת בְּעֵינֵי יַהְוֶה”: this is a light thing in Yahweh's eyes; he will also give Moab into your hand.
Hezekiah: “נָקֵל לַצֵּל לִנְטוֹת עֶשֶׂר מַעֲלוֹת”: it is easy for the shadow to go down ten steps; let it go back.
“Knowledge לְנָבוֹן נָקָל”, is easy to him who understands.
“נָקֵל מִהְיוֹתְךָ לִי עֶבֶד”: it is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob; I will give you for a light of the nations.
David: “הַנְקַלָּה בְעֵינֵיכֶם”, does it seem a light thing to you to be the king's son-in-law?
As if it had been a light thing for Ahab to walk in Jeroboam's sins, he took Jezebel and served Baal.
“הֲנָקֵל לְבֵית יְהוּדָה”: is it a light thing to the house of Judah to do these abominations?

senses.definition: The feminine participle with עַל: lightly, as though the matter were slight.

evidence.note: “They have healed the breach of my people עַל־נְקַלָּה, saying, Peace, peace, and there is no peace.”

senses.definition: To become of less account, set beside being low (שָׁפָל) and against being honoured.

evidence.note: David to Michal: “וּנְקַלֹּתִי עוֹד מִזֹּאת וְהָיִיתִי שָׁפָל בְּעֵינָי”, but with the maidservants “אִכָּבֵדָה”, I shall be honoured.

senses.definition: To show oneself swift, of pursuers.

evidence.note: “וְעַל־קַל נִרְכָּב עַל־כֵּן יִקַּלּוּ רֹדְפֵיכֶם”: we will ride on the swift; therefore your pursuers shall be swift.

senses.gloss: revile, treat with contempt (parents, rulers, God, the deaf)
senses.definition: To make light of one who should be honoured, by speaking against him: father and mother, the ruler, God himself. It is set against כַּבֵּד “honour” and beside אָרַר; reviling father or mother, or God, was a capital offence.

evidence.note: “וּמְקַלֵּל אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ מוֹת יוּמָת”, against the command “כַּבֵּד אֶת־אָבִיךָ וְאֶת־אִמֶּךָ” (Exo 20:12).
Jesus quotes Exo 20:12 and 21:17 together: “honour your father and mother, and ὁ κακολογῶν πατέρα ἢ μητέρα let him die the death”; also Mrk 7:10.
“אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ קִלֵּל דָּמָיו בּוֹ.”
“אֱלֹהִים לֹא תְקַלֵּל וְנָשִׂיא בְעַמְּךָ לֹא תָאֹר”: קִלֵּל parallel to אָרַר.
The son of the Israelite woman “blasphemed the Name, וַיְקַלֵּל”.
“Whoever יְקַלֵּל אֱלֹהָיו shall bear his sin.”
They brought “הַמְקַלֵּל” outside the camp and stoned him.
“לֹא־תְקַלֵּל חֵרֵשׁ”, nor put a stumbling block before the blind.
Eli's sons “מְקַלְלִים לָהֶם”, made themselves vile, and he did not restrain them.
Abishai: Shimei should die “כִּי קִלֵּל אֶת־מְשִׁיחַ יַהְוֶה”.
“מְקַלֵּל אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ, his lamp shall be put out.”
“A generation that curses its father and does not bless its mother.”
The hungry man “וְקִלֵּל בְּמַלְכּוֹ וּבֵאלֹהָיו”.
“Do not curse the king even in your thought.”

senses.definition: To speak a curse against someone, wishing or calling down evil on him, often by a god's name; the opposite of בֵּרַךְ “bless”. When Yahweh is the one who curses, the curse falls.

evidence.note: “וַאֲבָרֲכָה מְבָרְכֶיךָ וּמְקַלֶּלְךָ אָאֹר”: I will bless those who bless you, and him who curses you I will curse (אָרַר).
“יְקַלְלוּ־הֵמָּה וְאַתָּה תְבָרֵךְ”: let them curse, but you bless.
“With their mouth they bless (יְבָרֵכוּ), and inwardly they curse (יְקַלְלוּ).”
“וַיְקַלֵּל הַפְּלִשְׁתִּי אֶת־דָּוִד בֵּאלֹהָיו”: Goliath cursed David by his gods.
Elisha “וַיְקַלְלֵם בְּשֵׁם יַהְוֶה”, and two she-bears came out of the wood.
Balaam was hired “לְקַלְלֶךָּ”, to curse Israel; Yahweh turned the curse into a blessing (Deu 23:6).
Shimei came out “יֹצֵא יָצוֹא וּמְקַלֵּל”; his curse was “Get out, get out, man of blood” (2Sa 16:7), with stones and dust (2Sa 16:13).
David: “if Yahweh said to him, קַלֵּל אֶת־דָּוִד, who shall say, Why have you done so?”
“He cursed me with a grievous curse (קְלָלָה נִמְרֶצֶת).”
Yahweh: “לֹא־אֹסִף לְקַלֵּל עוֹד אֶת־הָאֲדָמָה” for man's sake.
The men of Shechem ate and drank in their god's house and cursed Abimelech.
“Job opened his mouth וַיְקַלֵּל אֶת־יוֹמוֹ.”
Nehemiah contended with those who married foreign wives “and cursed them”.
“Every one of them curses me.”
Do not slander a servant to his master, “lest he curse you”.
Do not heed every word, lest you hear your servant cursing you; you know you yourself have cursed others.

senses.definition: Passive of the piel: to be under a curse, set against being blessed.

evidence.note: “מְבֹרָכָיו יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ וּמְקֻלָּלָיו יִכָּרֵתוּ”: those blessed by him shall inherit the land, and those cursed by him shall be cut off.
“וְהַחוֹטֶא בֶּן־מֵאָה שָׁנָה יְקֻלָּל”: the sinner a hundred years old shall be cursed.
“תְּקֻלַּל חֶלְקָתָם בָּאָרֶץ”: their portion is cursed in the earth.

stems.gloss: make light, lighten; treat with contempt

senses.gloss: make light, lighten (a load, a yoke, a hand, a ship)
senses.definition: To make a weight lighter or take it off: the burden of judging, a heavy yoke, Yahweh's hand, a ship's cargo. Usually with מֵעַל “from upon”.

evidence.note: “Your father made our yoke hard; now הָקֵל מֵעֲבֹדַת אָבִיךָ הַקָּשָׁה וּמֵעֻלּוֹ הַכָּבֵד”: lighten the hard service and the heavy yoke.
“אָבִיךָ הִכְבִּיד אֶת־עֻלֵּנוּ וְאַתָּה הָקֵל מֵעָלֵינוּ”: heavy set against light.
Jethro: let the judges hear the small matters, “וְהָקֵל מֵעָלֶיךָ וְנָשְׂאוּ אִתָּךְ”, so lighten it from you and they will bear it with you.
The Philistines: give glory to the God of Israel; “perhaps יָקֵל אֶת־יָדוֹ מֵעֲלֵיכֶם”.
The sailors threw the cargo into the sea “לְהָקֵל מֵעֲלֵיהֶם”.

senses.gloss: treat as light, bring into contempt
senses.definition: To make a person or land of no account, to dishonour; set against הִכְבִּיד “make heavy, glorious” and beside חִלֵּל “profane”.

evidence.note: “כָּעֵת הָרִאשׁוֹן הֵקַל אַרְצָה זְבֻלוּן וְאַרְצָה נַפְתָּלִי וְהָאַחֲרוֹן הִכְבִּיד”: at first he brought them into contempt, at the last he made them glorious; Matthew sees it fulfilled when Jesus dwelt in Galilee (Mat 4:13–16).
Yahweh purposed “לְחַלֵּל גְּאוֹן כָּל־צְבִי לְהָקֵל כָּל־נִכְבַּדֵּי־אָרֶץ”: to profane the pride and bring into contempt all the honoured of the earth.
The men of Israel to Judah: “וּמַדּוּעַ הֱקִלֹּתַנִי”, why did you despise us?
“אָב וָאֵם הֵקַלּוּ בָךְ”: father and mother they have made light of in you.

senses.definition: To shake to and fro, of arrows shaken in divination.

evidence.note: The king of Babylon at the fork of the road “קִלְקַל בַּחִצִּים”, shook the arrows, asked the teraphim, looked in the liver.

senses.definition: Of iron: to whet or polish the edge. The sense is from the context; how it goes back to the root's lightness is not clear.

evidence.note: “If the iron is blunt וְהוּא לֹא־פָנִים קִלְקַל”, and one has not whetted the edge, he must use more strength.

stems.gloss: be shaken, move to and fro

senses.gloss: move lightly to and fro, be shaken
senses.definition: Of the hills in Jeremiah's vision of the land undone: to move to and fro, parallel to רָעַשׁ “quake”.

evidence.note: “I looked at the mountains, and behold, רֹעֲשִׁים, and all the hills הִתְקַלְקָלוּ.”

evidence.locator: Lev.24.11, וַיְקַלֵּל → κατηράσατο; 2Sa.16.5, מְקַלֵּל → καταρώμενος; Psa.109.28, יְקַלְלוּ → καταράσονται; Ecc.10.20, תְּקַלֵּל → καταράση

evidence.note: “Bless those who curse you (τοὺς καταρωμένους ὑμῖν)”: the reverse of curse for curse, as in Psa 109:28, “let them curse, but you bless”.
“Bless, and do not curse (μὴ καταρᾶσθε).”
With the tongue we bless God and curse men made in his likeness: out of one mouth come blessing and curse.

evidence.locator: Exo.21.17, מְקַלֵּל → κακολογῶν; Exo.22.27, תְקַלֵּל → κακολογήσεις; 1Sa.3.13, מְקַלְלִים → κακολογοῦντες

evidence.note: Exo 21:17 quoted: “ὁ κακολογῶν πατέρα ἢ μητέρα θανάτῳ τελευτάτω.”
The same quotation, as the word of Moses.

evidence.locator: Jon.1.5, לְהָקֵל → κουφισθῆναι; 1Ki.12.4, הָקֵל → κούφισον; 1Sa.6.5, יָקֵל → κουφίσῃ; Exo.18.22 → κουφιοῦσιν

evidence.note: “They lightened the ship (ἐκούφιζον τὸ πλοῖον), throwing the wheat into the sea”, as the sailors did in Jon 1:5; the Peshitta has the same root, אַקֵלו.

parallels.note: “Curse”, the other verb for cursing, beside קִלֵּל in the same law and the same promise.

evidence.note: “וּמְקַלֶּלְךָ אָאֹר”: him who makes light of you I will curse.

parallels.note: “Despise”: those who despise Yahweh shall be made light.
“Profane”: to profane pride is to bring the honoured into contempt.

opposites.note: “Bless”: the constant opposite of the piel.

evidence.note: The pual “cursed” against “blessed”.

opposites.note: “Be heavy, honour”: lightness is the opposite of weight, and contempt of honour.

evidence.note: “מְכַבְּדַי אֲכַבֵּד וּבֹזַי יֵקָלּוּ.”
הֵקַל against הִכְבִּיד.
הִכְבִּיד אֶת־עֻלֵּנוּ against הָקֵל.
“כַּבֵּד אֶת־אָבִיךָ וְאֶת־אִמֶּךָ” against מְקַלֵּל אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ (Exo 21:17).

phrases.gloss: a light thing in the eyes of, easy for

evidence.note: The qal with בְּעֵינֶיהָ: despised in her eyes.

phrases.gloss: lighten from upon, take a weight off

words.summary: The noun of the piel, thirty-three times: a curse spoken, the curse of the covenant set before Israel beside the blessing, and a people or city become a curse, a byword of cursing among the nations. Its constant opposite is בְּרָכָה “blessing”.

senses.definition: Words calling down evil on someone, the opposite of a blessing; a curse without cause does not land, and Yahweh can turn it to blessing.

evidence.note: Jacob: “I shall bring on myself קְלָלָה וְלֹא בְרָכָה.”
Rebekah: “עָלַי קִלְלָתְךָ בְּנִי.”
“As a bird wandering, as a swallow flying, כֵּן קִלְלַת חִנָּם לֹא תָבֹא.”
Yahweh would not listen to Balaam, “וַיַּהֲפֹךְ יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהֶיךָ לְּךָ אֶת־הַקְּלָלָה לִבְרָכָה כִּי אֲהֵבְךָ”.
“וַיַּהֲפֹךְ אֱלֹהֵינוּ הַקְּלָלָה לִבְרָכָה.”
David: perhaps Yahweh will look on my affliction and repay me good “תַּחַת קִלְלָתוֹ הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה”.
“קְלָלָה נִמְרֶצֶת”, a grievous curse.
God returned the evil of Shechem on their heads, “and on them came קִלְלַת יוֹתָם”.
“He loved קְלָלָה and it came to him; he did not delight in בְרָכָה and it was far from him.”
“He clothed himself with cursing as with his garment.”
He who blesses his friend with a loud voice early in the morning, “קְלָלָה תֵּחָשֶׁב לוֹ”.

senses.definition: The evil that the law of Moses set before Israel as the consequence of disobedience, beside the blessing for obedience; written in the book and read aloud on Mount Ebal.

evidence.note: “רְאֵה אָנֹכִי נֹתֵן לִפְנֵיכֶם הַיּוֹם בְּרָכָה וּקְלָלָה.”
“וְהַקְּלָלָה אִם־לֹא תִשְׁמְעוּ אֶל־מִצְוֹת יַהְוֶה”, and turn to go after other gods.
The blessing on Mount Gerizim, the curse on Mount Ebal.
“If you will not listen to the voice of Yahweh … כָּל־הַקְּלָלוֹת הָאֵלֶּה shall come upon you.”
“כָּל־הַקְּלָלָה הַכְּתוּבָה בַּסֵּפֶר הַזֶּה.”
When the blessing and the curse have come on you among the nations, and you return.
“הַחַיִּים וְהַמָּוֶת נָתַתִּי לְפָנֶיךָ הַבְּרָכָה וְהַקְּלָלָה וּבָחַרְתָּ בַּחַיִּים”: life and death, the blessing and the curse; choose life.
Joshua read “הַבְּרָכָה וְהַקְּלָלָה” as written in the book of the law.
Paul: those of the works of the law are “ὑπὸ κατάραν”, under a curse.

senses.gloss: a curse, an object of cursing, a byword
senses.definition: A person, people or city so struck by judgment that it becomes the example men curse by; with הָיָה לְ or נָתַן לְ, beside “horror”, “reproach”, “hissing”. Also the hanged man, who is “the curse of God”.

evidence.note: “From them shall be taken up קְלָלָה by all the exiles of Judah: Yahweh make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted (קָלָם) in the fire”: the curse is the formula that names them.
“לְחֶרְפָּה וּלְמָשָׁל לִשְׁנִינָה וְלִקְלָלָה”, in all the places where I drive them.
Jerusalem and the cities of Judah “לְחָרְבָּה לְשַׁמָּה לִשְׁרֵקָה וְלִקְלָלָה”.
“This city I will make לִקְלָלָה to all the nations of the earth.”
Bozrah shall become a desolation, a reproach, a waste and a curse.
This place and its people “לִהְיוֹת לְשַׁמָּה וְלִקְלָלָה”.
“As you were קְלָלָה among the nations, house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you, and you shall be בְּרָכָה.”
The body shall not remain on the tree, “כִּי־קִלְלַת אֱלֹהִים תָּלוּי”: a hanged man is the curse of God.
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, γενόμενος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατάρα”, quoting Deu 21:23: “ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ὁ κρεμάμενος ἐπὶ ξύλου.”

evidence.locator: Gen.27.12, קְלָלָה → κατάραν; Deu.11.26 → κατάραν; Deu.30.19 → κατάραν; κατάρα renders קְלָלָה ×23; at Deu.21.23 קִלְלַת → κεκατηραμένος

evidence.note: Christ “became a curse (κατάρα) for us”, from Deu 21:23.
“As many as are of the works of the law are under a curse (ὑπὸ κατάραν).”
“Out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing (εὐλογία καὶ κατάρα).”
Land that bears thorns and thistles is rejected and “near to a curse (κατάρας ἐγγύς)”, as the land that drinks the rain and brings forth the blessing (Heb 6:7).

parallels.note: “Curse, oath”, in Jeremiah's lists of what Judah will become.

opposites.note: “Blessing”: the curse and the blessing are set side by side throughout.

phrases.gloss: the curse of God (said of the hanged man)
turn the curse into a blessing
the blessing and the curse (of the covenant)
become a curse, a byword of cursing

words.summary: Thirteen times, nearly always of speed: the man light of foot, the swift runner, horse, camel, messenger or cloud. Used as an adverb, “swiftly”.

senses.definition: Light in movement, quick: of runners and warriors, beasts, messengers, a cloud. The swift is set beside the mighty (גִּבּוֹר), and neither escapes when Yahweh judges.

evidence.note: “וַעֲשָׂהאֵל קַל בְּרַגְלָיו כְּאַחַד הַצְּבָיִם אֲשֶׁר בַּשָּׂדֶה”: Asahel was light of foot as a gazelle in the field.
“וְקַל בְּרַגְלָיו לֹא יְמַלֵּט”: the swift of foot shall not deliver himself.
“Flight shall perish מִקָּל.”
“אַל־יָנוּס הַקַּל וְאַל־יִמָּלֵט הַגִּבּוֹר.”
“לֹא לַקַּלִּים הַמֵּרוֹץ וְלֹא לַגִּבּוֹרִים הַמִּלְחָמָה”: the race is not to the swift.
“קַלִּים הָיוּ רֹדְפֵינוּ מִנִּשְׁרֵי שָׁמָיִם.”
“לְכוּ מַלְאָכִים קַלִּים”, go, swift messengers.
“הִנֵּה יַהְוֶה רֹכֵב עַל־עָב קַל וּבָא מִצְרַיִם”: Yahweh rides on a swift cloud.
“וְעַל־קַל נִרְכָּב”: we will ride on the swift (horse).
“בִּכְרָה קַלָּה מְשָׂרֶכֶת דְּרָכֶיהָ”: a swift young camel running here and there.
“קַל־הוּא עַל־פְּנֵי־מַיִם”: he is swift (or light) on the face of the waters.

senses.definition: Beside מְהֵרָה “quickly”: swiftly, speedily.

evidence.note: Yahweh whistles for a nation from the end of the earth, “וְהִנֵּה מְהֵרָה קַל יָבוֹא”.
“קַל מְהֵרָה אָשִׁיב גְּמֻלְכֶם בְּרֹאשְׁכֶם.”

evidence.locator: Job.24.18, קַל → ἐλαφρός; elsewhere κοῦφος (2Sa.1.23 κοῦφοι for the verb), which the New Testament does not use

evidence.note: “My yoke is easy and my burden is light (ἐλαφρόν)”; the Peshitta has קַלִּילָא. Set against the heavy yoke the people asked Rehoboam to make light (1Ki 12:4).
“The momentary lightness (ἐλαφρόν) of our affliction” works an eternal weight (βάρος) of glory: light against heavy, as קַל against כָּבֵד.

parallels.note: “Mighty man”: the swift and the mighty side by side.

words.summary: Once, the people's word for the manna: the reduplicated form of the root, “very light”, of no worth.

senses.definition: Of no substance or worth: said in contempt of the bread from heaven.

evidence.note: “There is no bread and no water, וְנַפְשֵׁנוּ קָצָה בַּלֶּחֶם הַקְּלֹקֵל”: our soul loathes this worthless bread.

words.summary: Once, in Habakkuk's woe on the Chaldean: a strengthened form of shame, set against כָּבוֹד “glory” and beside קָלוֹן “shame” in the same verse.

senses.definition: Shame that replaces glory: being made of no weight before others.

evidence.note: “שָׂבַעְתָּ קָלוֹן מִכָּבוֹד … תִּסּוֹב עָלֶיךָ כּוֹס יְמִין יַהְוֶה וְקִיקָלוֹן עַל־כְּבוֹדֶךָ”: the cup of Yahweh's right hand, and utter shame on your glory.

words.summary: Twice, in the phrase נְחֹשֶׁת קָלָל, “burnished bronze”, of the feet of the living creatures and of the man in linen. The sense is fixed by the context, gleaming; it goes with the pilpel “whet, polish” (Ecc 10:10), but how either goes back to the root's lightness is not clear, and no cognate yet supports it, so it stands on two verses and its context.

senses.definition: Of bronze: polished so that it gleams.

evidence.note: The feet of the living creatures “וְנֹצְצִים כְּעֵין נְחֹשֶׁת קָלָל”, sparkling like the gleam of burnished bronze.
The man clothed in linen: “his arms and feet כְּעֵין נְחֹשֶׁת קָלָל, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude”.
The same figure in John's vision: feet “like fine bronze, as if burned in a furnace”, and a voice “as the sound of many waters”.

words.summary: Once if at all: Jer 3:9, “מִקֹּל זְנוּתָהּ”, read “through the lightness of her harlotry”. The spelling is also a defective spelling of קוֹל “voice”, and the verse can be read “from the report of her harlotry”, so the word rests on one uncertain verse. It has no `bdb` key here: its key's tokens are all spellings shared with קוֹל, which belongs to another root, and counting them would credit it with five hundred uses of “voice”.

senses.definition: Lightness of conduct: Judah treated her harlotry as a light thing.

evidence.note: “וְהָיָה מִקֹּל זְנוּתָהּ וַתֶּחֱנַף אֶת־הָאָרֶץ וַתִּנְאַף אֶת־הָאֶבֶן וְאֶת־הָעֵץ.”

words.summary: The Peshitta's verb of the root, ܩܠ; in the aphel “make light”, of the ship in Paul's voyage, where the Greek has κουφίζω.

senses.definition: To make a ship lighter by throwing cargo overboard.

evidence.note: “וכַד סבַעו מֵאכֻולתָּא אַקֵלו מֵן אֵלפָא”: when they had eaten enough they lightened the ship and threw the wheat into the sea; compare לְהָקֵל in Jon 1:5.

words.summary: The Peshitta's adjective of the root, ܩܠܝܠܐ: light in weight, and as an adverb “a little”, of distance or time, where the Greek has ἐλαφρός or μικρόν.

senses.definition: Light in weight, of a burden or affliction, set against what is heavy.

evidence.note: “נִירי גֵּיר בַּסִים הו ומַובַּלי קַלִילָא הי”: my yoke is pleasant and my burden is light.
The affliction of this time, “זעֻור וקַלִיל”, small and light, works for us a great glory.

senses.definition: As an adverb: a little way, a little while.

evidence.note: In Gethsemane “וַפרַק קַלִיל וַנפַל עַל אַפַּוהי”: he went a little further and fell on his face.
“קַלִיל ולָא תֵּחזֻונָני ותֻוב קַלִיל ותֵחזֻונָני”: a little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me.

cognates.gloss: be(come) light; be(come) unimportant; belittle, despise, vilify; diminish
cognates.note: The same verb with the same range: light in weight, of little account, and, in the D stem (uqallil, as the Hebrew piel), to belittle, despise and vilify. It joins the Hebrew's lightness to its making light of and reviling.

evidence.note: Meanings: be(come) light, be(come) unimportant, be(come) vilified, belittle, defile, despise, diminish, humiliating, reduce; forms include iqallil, uqallil, qullulu; 89 instances.

cognates.gloss: light; little, small; underweight; unimportant person
cognates.note: The adjective, as קַל: light in weight, and small or of little account.

evidence.note: Meanings: light, little, small, tiny, underweight, unimportant person, slave, boy, a unit of weight; 385 instances.

cognates.note: A noun of qalālu, “disgrace”, as קִיקָלוֹן is the Hebrew's noun of disgrace.

evidence.note: Meanings: belittlement, disgrace; Neo-Assyrian, 22 instances.

cognates.note: The D-stem adjective “despised”, as קְלֹקֵל is a strengthened form for what is worthless.

evidence.note: Meaning: despised.
Meaning: despicable person.

cognates.gloss: be few, little, small; (II) make or hold to be little; (V) deem little; qalīl few, little
cognates.note: Arabic keeps the root's slightness as smallness of amount: to be few or little, and in the second stem (qallala, formed as the piel) to make or hold a thing to be little. It shares the Hebrew's “of little account” and the Peshitta's קַלִּיל “a little”; it does not show the sense of speed or of cursing.

evidence.note: “It was, or became, few; small, or little, in number, quantity, or amount; scanty”; (2) “He made it, or held it, to be little”; (5) “He saw it, or deemed it, to be little”; قَلِيلٌ “Few; small, or little”.

cognates.gloss: be light; be of light esteem; be reduced; (pael) be quick, pass swiftly; make light, ease (Jewish Aramaic)
cognates.note: The Targums use it where the Hebrew has קָלַל: Onkelos at Gen 16:4 (Sarai light in Hagar's eyes) and at Gen 8:8, 11 (the waters lightened), and the pael at Job 7:6 and 9:25 (days swifter than a runner).

evidence.note: “to be light; to be of light esteem. Targ. O. Gen. XVI, 4 … to be reduced. Ib. VIII, 8; 11”; Pa. “to be quick, to pass swiftly. Targ. Job VII, 6; IX, 25 … to make light; trnsf. to ease, relieve”.

cognates.note: The Targums' word for קַל at 2Sa 2:18 (Asahel light of foot) and Jer 2:23 (the swift camel).

evidence.note: “= h. קַל, light of weight; quick. Targ. II Sam. II, 18 … Targ. Jer. II, 23; a. fr.”

cognates.gloss: be light (in weight); be tolerable, easy; be swift, quick
cognates.note: Ge'ez has both the Hebrew's senses of lightness: light in weight and easy, and swift.

evidence.note: “to be light (in weight); to be tolerable, convenient”; “to be light (in weight); to be swift, quick”.

evidence.locator: SEM001080 qll [slight] V, GEZ004282 qll [light] V

evidence.note: Ethiopic “light, easy”, with a causative “belittle, vilify, hold in contempt (as Heb, Syr)” (OCR read; PDF not rendered).

doctrine.statement: The law said that when a man guilty of death was put to death and hanged on a tree, his body must not stay there overnight, “for a hanged man is the curse of God (קִלְלַת אֱלֹהִים)” (Deu 21:22–23). The apostles preached that the Jews killed Jesus “hanging him on a tree”, and that God raised him up (Act 5:30; 10:39); the Jews asked Pilate that the bodies not remain on the cross over the Sabbath (Jhn 19:31). Paul says that all who are of the works of the law are under a curse, and that “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us”, quoting the same verse, “cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree”, “so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations in Christ Jesus” (Gal 3:10, 13–14). God sent his son “born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law” (Gal 4:4–5); he “did no sin” (1Pe 2:22), and “bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1Pe 2:24). From the verses: Jesus, a man born under the law, died the death the law named as God's curse, though he had done no sin; God raised him, and in him the curse of the law is ended for those who belong to him, and the blessing promised to Abraham reaches the nations.

Yahweh told Abram, “I will bless those who bless you, and him who curses you (מְקַלֶּלְךָ) I will curse” (Gen 12:3), and Paul calls the promise that in him all nations shall be blessed the gospel preached beforehand (Gal 3:8). When Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, Yahweh would not listen to Balaam but “turned the curse into a blessing, because Yahweh your God loved you” (Deu 23:5–6; Neh 13:2). David bore Shimei's cursing, saying that Yahweh might repay him good for it (2Sa 16:10–12); the psalmist says, “let them curse, but you bless” (Psa 109:28); and “a curse without cause does not come” (Pro 26:2). Jesus tells his disciples to bless those who curse them (Luk 6:28), Paul to “bless and do not curse” (Rom 12:14), Peter not to return reviling for reviling but blessing (1Pe 3:9), and James that blessing and cursing should not come from one mouth (Jas 3:9–10). From the verses: the curse of men cannot harm those whom Yahweh blesses, and he turns it to their good, so those he has blessed answer cursing with blessing.

Moses set before Israel the blessing and the curse (Deu 11:26; 30:19) and said that when both had come on them among the nations to which Yahweh had driven them, and they returned to him, he would gather them again from all the peoples (Deu 30:1–3). The prophets saw Judah become “a curse” in all the places to which they were driven (Jer 24:9; 44:8). Zechariah answers it: “as you were a curse among the nations, house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you, and you shall be a blessing” (Zec 8:13). From the verses: Israel's scattering under the curse is not the end of the covenant; the same law that named the curse promised the regathering, and the prophets name the nation that was a curse as the nation Yahweh will save and make a blessing.

In Isaiah's new heavens and new earth Yahweh rejoices in Jerusalem, and weeping is heard there no more (Isa 65:17–19); “the youth shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be cursed (יְקֻלָּל)” (Isa 65:20); men build houses and live in them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit (Isa 65:21), and bear children who are “the seed of the blessed of Yahweh” (Isa 65:23); the wolf and the lamb feed together in all his holy mountain (Isa 65:25). Paul says Christ must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet, and the last enemy destroyed is death (1Co 15:25–26). From the verses: the age Isaiah describes is on the earth, with a people who still build, plant, bear children and die, though at a great age, and among whom sin is still cursed; it is Christ's reign before death itself is ended.

note: Root key קלל, BDB's own key for the words, so the entry joins to them; no other entry has it. קוֹל “voice” is left out: lexicon-brief files it here under the spelling קֹל (s.br.ac, 506 tokens), but every one of those surfaces is shared with s.au.ab, BDB's קוֹל under קול, and the cognates put “voice” under its own root q-w-l: Ugaritic ql /qol-/ “voice” glossed with Arabic qawl (Segert 1984, p. 199, §93 Glossary), Phoenician QL “voice” (Krahmalkov 2000, p. 426), Ge'ez qāl “voice, speech, sound” (Fisher 1969, p. 174, *qwl), Anderson and Moser *qwl. It should have its own entry (root קול, s.au.ab). The word קֹל “lightness” (Jer 3:9) is kept without a bdb key for that reason; s.br.ac is left unclaimed, and if the קול entry claims nothing for it either, the word sheet will not show this entry on קוֹל tokens. קָלוֹן “shame” is not filed here: BDB files it under קלה (s.bo.ab) and qali.json has it with the “held light” words of קלה; the two roots overlap in sense (Akkadian qalālu, qulālu), and Hab 2:16 sets קָלוֹן and קִיקָלוֹן side by side. Jer 29:22 plays קְלָלָה against קָלָם “roasted” (קלה). Cross-reference keys with no tokens claimed: s.bm.am on קַל, s.bm.ae on קִיקָלוֹן, s.bu.ac on קְלֹקֵל; s.bq.ad goes with the name Kallai. The pilpel, hithpalpel and קָלָל carry no cognate: “shake” and “polish” may be the root's lightness (what is light moves easily; a polished surface?), but that is not shown; leads: Fisher 1969 pp. 175–176 compares the Hebrew pilpel “shake” with Ethiopic forms (OCR unclear). Ugaritic is left out: Segert p. 199 lists a verb “to fall” under /q-w-l/, /q-y-l/ or /q-l-l/(?), and Fisher pp. 175–176 seems to read Ugaritic qll “fall” with a noun “shame” (OCR unclear); check the scans before citing. Phoenician QLL (Krahmalkov p. 426) is “vessel, pitcher”, not this root's sense. Leads not followed: Payne Smith and Brockelmann for Syriac ܩܠ, ܩܠܝܠܐ and the aphel participle מַקלִין at Gal 5:26 (Greek προκαλούμενοι, “provoking”), whose sense needs checking; Dillmann and Leslau for Ge'ez ቀለለ by column and page; the Targums' word for the piel “curse” (Onkelos uses other roots?). Ezk 21:26 and Ecc 10:10 are the only pilpel verses; the sense “whet” rests on context.
